vignette:
Kwame, a 20-year-old doctor, had been deployed as a field medic in a volatile region when his life fractured. He remembered the deafening thud of the mortar round, followed by an unnerving, complete silence that descended over the makeshift clinic. He was trying to stabilize a young boy with shrapnel wounds, his own chest tightening with a profound difficulty breathing as he worked amidst the chaos. The image of the boy’s contorted face, and the senseless violence that had brought him there, became etched in his mind, even as other details blurred.

Back home, the experience had left Kwame feeling like a stranger to himself; he often thought, "I don't know myself anymore." He found himself constantly on edge, feeling he "had to be on guard all the time," a pervasive sense of hypervigilance that permeated every aspect of his life. This constant need to be vigilant meant that any sudden silence in the hospital corridors, or a patient struggling with breathlessness during rounds, would immediately trigger an overwhelming cascade of fear and dread. These triggers would reinforce his belief that his understanding of the world had been completely shattered, leading him to conclude that his "beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed."

His internal world became a battleground, particularly when it came to the traumatic event itself. When he tried to grasp what happened, the pervasive feeling that he "had to be on guard all the time" made him push the memory away before he could fully recall it, convinced that confronting the full horror would shatter him entirely. As a result, his memories of the event came only in disconnected, fragmented pieces that refused to fit together, leaving significant memory gaps he simply couldn't fill, no matter how hard he tried. This struggle with his own memory, the fragmented pieces and the parts he simply couldn't remember, fueled his profound sense of identity loss, leaving him questioning who he was meant to be now. The very act of trying to recall a fragmented piece of memory could, in an instant, make him feel a familiar difficulty breathing, or react with a jolt to a sudden silence in the room, as if he were back in the midst of the conflict.

Kwame’s occupation as a doctor, once his greatest passion, now felt like a constant exposure to threat. The quiet hum of an operating room could suddenly become an oppressive silence, causing his breath to catch, and the sight of a patient in distress struggling to breathe would send a jolt of panic through him, making him fear he was reliving the war. His pervasive hypervigilance, the certainty that he "had to be on guard all the time," made him interpret even minor hospital disputes as potential violence, leading him to isolate himself from colleagues and patients alike. He had started avoiding the emergency department, where the risk of encountering unexpected violence or medical emergencies mirroring his past trauma was highest. This constant state of alert, driven by his shattered beliefs, meant that his sensitivity to potential triggers was amplified; any minor disruption could send him into a spiral of anxiety, making even the most benign moments feel dangerous.

The accumulating weight of his fragmented memories and the feeling that he "didn't know himself anymore" had begun to impact his professional competence. He found himself making small errors, his focus constantly pulled away by intrusive thoughts or the need to scan his environment. He was certain his beliefs about the world had been completely destroyed, and this made him question his ability to heal others when he felt so broken himself. Exhausted by the incessant need to be on guard, and haunted by the knowledge that there were parts of the event he simply couldn't remember, Kwame finally sought help. He desperately wanted to reclaim the person he once was, but what frightened him most was the possibility that there was nothing left to reclaim.
